title: Everything rhymes with porcelain - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Porcelain is both one of humanity's oldest high technologies and, through engineered ceramics like Cosentino's Dekton, one of its newest. The author argues that materials science is quietly transforming the physical world as profoundly as digital tech and AI, though its incremental innovations make it nearly invisible.

insights.claim: Extreme pressure and heat cause atoms in kaolinite and quartz particles to diffuse across their boundaries, turning Dekton into effectively a single solid mass and nearly eliminating porcelain's historic brittleness caused by microscopic voids acting as stress concentrators.

insights.so_what: Removing structural flaws turns a fragile luxury material into a durable functional one.

insights.claim: Porcelain forms when kaolin is fired to about 1,200 degrees centigrade, at which point silica breaks free and forms a liquid glass that fills a web of needle-shaped crystals, producing a dense, translucent matrix.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Understanding structure-property relationships is the core of materials science, even in ancient crafts.

insights.claim: Porcelain required a concatenation of innovations, including downdraft kilns that trapped heat via floor vents and new heat-resistant bricks that would not shatter or melt at high temperatures.

insights.so_what: Breakthrough materials depend on complementary process and equipment innovations.

insights.claim: European elites, resenting importers' high prices for Asian porcelain, spent lavishly for centuries trying to make their own and failed, largely because they did not know it was made from kaolin plus silicon-bearing 'China stone'.
